name: Algiers
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Algiers: state enterprise counterparties, the specialised commercial court, port trade and agent vetting.
hero_lede: Algiers is Algeria's political and economic capital, home to central ministries, state enterprises, banks and the main commercial port. Matters touching it often involve public sector counterparties, importers and intermediaries, and TDSC scopes research around the city's courts, registries and practical limits on access.
intro: Algiers is the capital of Algeria and the seat of its government, central administrations and principal financial institutions. The wilaya of Algiers is the country's most populous and smallest by area, with 57 communes and a population of about 3.15 million in 2015 according to the national investment portal. It concentrates around 40 percent of Algerian companies and close to a quarter of national GDP, and it attracts about a quarter of the foreign investment declared nationally. The Port of Algiers is the country's leading commercial port. Business districts range from the central city and the Bab Ezzouar technology and university zone to industrial areas at Rouiba and El Harrach.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Algiers because most significant dealings with Algeria pass through the capital. State-owned groups in energy, telecoms, construction and finance are headquartered there, and foreign suppliers and partners deal with their procurement departments and with intermediaries claiming influence over them. Importers, distributors and logistics companies based around the port are frequent counterparties for foreign manufacturers. Clients ask who owns an Algerian partner, whether an agent's claimed relationships are real, whether a company has been involved in corruption cases that have reached the Algiers courts in recent years, and what assets a counterparty holds if a dispute arises.

matters.title: State enterprise procurement counterparties
matters.text: Researching the Algerian partners, subcontractors and consortium members that foreign companies encounter when bidding for contracts with state-owned groups headquartered in Algiers, including ownership, links to officials, prior corruption proceedings and reputation, before bids are submitted or joint ventures are formed.

matters.title: Agent and intermediary verification
matters.text: Testing claims by consultants and commercial agents in Algiers that they can facilitate approvals, licences or contract awards, through company records, court reporting, Arabic and French press and discreet reputational enquiries by qualified local professionals, given the heightened anti-corruption exposure such intermediaries carry.

matters.title: Importer and distributor diligence
matters.text: Checking importers, distributors and freight operators working through the Port of Algiers, including registration status, shareholders, trading history and any customs or commercial disputes, for manufacturers appointing distributors or extending credit under Algeria's changing import rules.

matters.title: Corruption case and asset exposure
matters.text: Reviewing whether counterparties, their owners or related businesses have featured in the corruption prosecutions and asset confiscation proceedings that have been prominent in Algiers courts in recent years, so clients understand reputational and legal exposure before engaging.

matters.title: Dispute and arbitration support
matters.text: Assembling factual background, corporate histories and asset information for counsel in disputes with Algerian counterparties, whether before the specialised commercial court in Algiers or in international arbitration, recognising the practical limits on access to Algerian court files and administrative records.

local_context.title: Specialised commercial court
local_context.text: Law 22-13 of 12 July 2022 amended the Code of Civil and Administrative Procedure to create specialised commercial courts. Algeria has twelve, and the Algiers court covers Algiers, Bouira, Tizi Ouzou and Boumerdès. It hears disputes over commercial companies, insolvency, intellectual property, banking with merchants, maritime, air transport and insurance matters, and international trade. A judge sits with four commercial assessors, and conciliation before the court president is a mandatory step before a claim is admissible.

local_context.title: Arbitration in Algiers
local_context.text: Algeria has promoted commercial arbitration and mediation, and the Algerian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CACI), based in Algiers, has run training on arbitral procedure. In February 2026 the president of the Algiers Bar announced the creation of an Algerian dispute resolution centre focused on arbitration and mediation of commercial and investment disputes. Its institutional status and rules should be checked before relying on it. Many contracts with foreign parties still choose international arbitration outside Algeria.

local_context.title: Trade register and official bulletins
local_context.text: Companies register with the National Centre of the Trade Register (CNRC), whose central services are in Algiers, and statutory notices appear in the Official Bulletin of Legal Announcements. Extracts are commonly obtained through local representatives rather than online, and much documentation is in Arabic or French. Searches need the correct registered name and number, as transliteration of names between Arabic and French produces variations that can hide or merge records.

local_context.title: Government and state enterprises
local_context.text: As the capital, Algiers hosts the ministries, regulators and headquarters of the main public companies, including the national hydrocarbons, telecoms and banking groups. Procurement decisions, licences and approvals are therefore often centralised in the city. Public information on these bodies comes mainly from official announcements, the Official Journal and the press, and direct access to officials for investigative purposes is not appropriate.

tdsc_approach: TDSC handles Algiers matters from Nashville and has no presence in Algeria. Engagements start with a clear scope agreed with the client and, where needed, Algerian counsel, because access to court files and administrative records is generally limited to parties and their representatives, and enquiries touching officials or state enterprises are sensitive. Research relies on the trade register and official bulletins, Arabic and French press, international corporate and litigation records, and sanctions and adverse media screening. Any local record retrieval or reputational enquiries are carried out by qualified local professionals working within Algerian law, including the personal data protection law. TDSC excludes surveillance, contact with officials and pretext techniques.

faqs.q: Which court hears commercial disputes in Algiers?
faqs.a: Since Law 22-13 of 2022, disputes over companies, insolvency, intellectual property, banking, transport, insurance and international trade go to the specialised commercial court in Algiers, which also covers Bouira, Tizi Ouzou and Boumerdès. A judge sits with four commercial assessors, and parties must first attempt conciliation before the court president. Counsel advises on procedure.

faqs.q: Can TDSC obtain Algerian company records remotely?
faqs.a: Partly. Some information is available from the official bulletins, press and international databases, but trade register extracts and filings are usually obtained in person through local representatives, often in Arabic. TDSC coordinates retrieval through qualified local professionals where a client needs certified records, and states clearly what could not be obtained.

faqs.q: Why check whether a counterparty appears in corruption cases?
faqs.a: Algiers courts have handled numerous high-profile corruption prosecutions and asset confiscations in recent years, involving businesspeople and former officials. A counterparty linked to those cases may carry reputational, legal or asset-recovery exposure. TDSC reviews court reporting and official announcements and distinguishes convictions, ongoing cases and unproven allegations.

faqs.q: Is there a commercial arbitration centre in Algiers?
faqs.a: The Algerian Chamber of Commerce and Industry is active in promoting arbitration, and a new Algerian dispute resolution centre for arbitration and mediation was announced by the Algiers Bar in February 2026. Its operating status should be confirmed. Contracts with foreign parties frequently provide for international arbitration abroad, which TDSC takes into account when planning evidence research.

faqs.q: Can TDSC verify an agent's claimed access to Algiers ministries?
faqs.a: TDSC can test the claim against lawful sources: the agent's company records, past contracts reported in the press, litigation, reputation among informed local professionals and any adverse media. It does not approach officials or use pretext. Where claims rest only on asserted personal relationships, the report treats them as a significant risk indicator.
